Where it began

Brendan Ross Murray Taylor was born in Harare on 6 February 1986. At Lilfordia School, near the city, his cricket was looked after by Iain Campbell, whose son Alistair played Tests for Zimbabwe. He went on to St John's College, played in two Under-19 World Cups and was playing first-class cricket for Mashonaland A at 15. The following season he made 200 not out in the Logan Cup.

He was only 18 when he made his Test debut, against Sri Lanka on 6 May 2004. For a while he kept wicket for his country, too.

The player

His day of days as a young man came in the 2007 World Twenty20, when his 60 not out, along with a catch, a stumping and a run-out, helped Zimbabwe beat Australia. A year earlier he had won a one-day game against Bangladesh by hitting a six off the final ball.

He became captain in June 2011, and in Zimbabwe's first Test back that August he made 71 and 105 not out against Bangladesh at Harare. Only David Houghton had made a hundred in his first match as Zimbabwe's captain before him, and Zimbabwe won by 130 runs. Later that year he made a fourth-innings hundred against New Zealand. In April 2013 he made hundreds in both innings against Bangladesh, with 171 the bigger of the two, and in November 2018 he did it again. No Zimbabwean had done that twice before.

By November 2026 he had played 38 Tests between 2004 and 2026, making 2,633 runs at 37.61 with seven hundreds and 13 fifties. He held 27 catches in the field and three more with the gloves on, and he led Zimbabwe in 16 Tests.

What made him special

Taylor played shots other batsmen only thought about. His upper cut over third man and his ramp became his trademarks, and people often likened him to Andy Flower. He was also the man Zimbabwe leaned on. In one-day cricket his 11 hundreds took him past Alistair Campbell's Zimbabwe record, and twice he made hundreds in consecutive matches. At the 2015 World Cup his 433 runs set a record for a Zimbabwean at any World Cup, and Sunil Gavaskar rated his 138 against India among the finest one-day innings he had seen.

His off-spin was a more modest weapon. He bowled in Tests without ever taking a wicket, though not for want of trying.

Away from the middle

He took his batting around the world, playing Twenty20 cricket in New Zealand and in Bangladesh, where he took over as captain of the Chittagong Kings partway through a season and steered them into the final. His form in 2011 earned him awards as both cricketer and batsman of the year. In October 2020 he made his 17th hundred for his country, the most by any Zimbabwean across the three formats at the time.

And finally

Six to win off the last ball is the stuff of back-garden dreams. Taylor got to live it for real at 20, and then spent the next twenty years making the improbable look rather ordinary.
